That caution can now be withdrawn: a shipped guest driver > issues exactly this sequence, by construction, for secondary-bus config cycles. **THE FIX, now backed by the driver rather than by reading the fork's comment:** } else { bus = (tag >> 16) & 0xff; /* type-1: bus is bits 23..16 */ dev = (tag >> 11) & 0x1f; /* type-1: device is bits 15..11 */ } **WHAT IS STILL NOT SETTLED, and every seat agrees:** the discriminating row. grok -- *"the witness address is not a type-1 tag, and empty-slot data cannot pin the extract"*; glm -- the row *"conflates IMPLEMENT with explicit-all-ones DECLINE, silent with latched, and can false-pass on stale all-ones unless the destination register is pre-seeded"*; the kimi substitute and minimax -- only a POPULATED bus-1 device could separate them. **Four independent routes to one wall.** glm's pre-seeding point is the one actionable improvement: seed the destination register so a stale all-ones cannot pass. *The lesson about this machine is the `ls _scratchpad/*.pdf` lesson again, one directory over: I declared a fact unverifiable while its primary source sat in the project. **Before calling a hardware question unanswerable here, look for the guest OS source tree.*** *** A FACT THIS ROW'S QUESTION DOES NOT CARRY, ESTABLISHED 2026-09-08 FROM THREE INDEPENDENT FILES: OPTION-SET MEMBER 5 (FAULT) IS NOT AVAILABLE ON ALPHA. *** This is an Alpha machine, and the adjudication of this row weighs dispositions from the standing option set. **FAULT looks available and is not**, which is the option-set-completeness problem inverted -- not a missing member, a PHANTOM one. memory_rw.c the device-failure dispatcher has MIPS and M88K exception arms and NO ALPHA ARM (found via dev_lca.c, `lcaisalane`) memory_alpha.c no MM-fault dispatch exists at all (found via `alphapteprot`) cpu_alpha_palcode ALPHA_KENTRY_MM and ALPHA_MMCSR_* are DEFINED and have NO CONSUMERS; kentry[] is written by wrent and initialised to a dummy PAL, never dispatched (found via `alphatbinegsel` Q3) **Three briefs reached this from three directions, none of them asked about it.** And a fourth seat priced it: choosing FAULT obliges building delivery first -- a PAL frame, `kentry[ALPHA_KENTRY_MM]`, MMCSR/VA, and teaching `pc_to_pointers` about a redirected PC. *"That is a new IMPLEMENT round, not a de-fatalisation."* > **SO ANY ANSWER TO THIS ROW THAT REACHES FOR FAULT IS REACHING FOR A ROUND THAT DOES NOT EXIST > YET.** It remains a legitimate ANSWER -- but it is an answer with a prerequisite, and the > prerequisite is large. Recorded here so the adjudication prices it rather than assuming it. *** THE NOTE ABOVE UNDERSTATED THE SCOPE, AND THE CORRECTION IS THE USEFUL PART: FAULT IS NOT "UNAVAILABLE ON ALPHA". IT IS AVAILABLE ON **MIPS AND M88K ONLY**, FOR EVERY ARCHITECTURE IN THIS TREE. Derived 2026-09-08 by opening the dispatcher. *** `src/cpus/memory_rw.c`, the device-failure path -- the whole of it: if (res <= 0 && !no_exceptions) { debug("[ %s device '%s' addr %08lx failed ]"); #ifdef MEM_MIPS mips_cpu_exception(cpu, cache == CACHE_INSTRUCTION? EXCEPTION_IBE : EXCEPTION_DBE, ...); #endif #ifdef MEM_M88K m88k_exception(cpu, cache == CACHE_INSTRUCTION ? M88K_EXCEPTION_INSTRUCTION_ACCESS : M88K_EXCEPTION_DATA_ACCESS, 0); #endif return MEMORY_ACCESS_FAILED; } **TWO `#ifdef` ARMS. There is no ARM arm, no Alpha arm, no PPC arm and no SH arm** -- every other architecture reaches `return MEMORY_ACCESS_FAILED` with no exception delivered at all. > **SO OPTION-SET MEMBER 5 IS A PHANTOM ON EVERY ARCHITECTURE BUT TWO**, and a round on an ARM, SH, > PPC or Alpha device that reaches for FAULT is reaching for a round that does not exist yet. *Found because I wrote the OPPOSITE into a brief. Assessing `fbfiqsilent` -- an ARM footbridge row -- I told the seat that "member 5 FAULT may genuinely be available here, `memory_rw`'s device-failure path has an ARM arm." It replied that the claimed arm **is absent from this tree**, and opening the file confirms it. **I was one brief away from spreading a false availability claim across the ARM queue**, having just corrected three rows for the Alpha version of it.* *** codex: REVISE. THE SHIFT IS RIGHT AND ALMOST EVERYTHING AROUND IT NEEDED CORRECTING -- INCLUDING TWO PREMISES I STATED AS SETTLED. *** **CONFIRMED, with a denominator.** `dev = (tag >> 11) & 0x1f` is correct: `relative_addr >> 5` undoes the address expansion, so for a valid tag T and aligned register R, `A = (T << 5) | (R << 5) | 24` gives `((A >> 5) & ~0xff) == T`, putting device bits at 15..11 of the recovered tag. Validated over **4,194,304 encode/decode combinations, zero mismatches** -- and codex labelled that an ARITHMETIC check, not an emulator test, which is the honest form. *** MY IMPLEMENT SKETCH WAS INCOMPLETE: IT DECODED `dev` AND NOT `bus`. *** `IOC_CONF` selects the CYCLE FORMAT, it does not supply the bus number -- PCI address bits 23..2 come from CPU address bits 28..7, and only bits 1..0 come from `IOC_CONF[1:0]`. So the minimum correction is } else { bus = (tag >> 16) & 0xff; dev = (tag >> 11) & 0x1f; } > **AND THE TRAP IN THE OBVIOUS ALTERNATIVE, which I would have walked into: DO NOT CHOOSE THE > DECODING BRANCH FROM THE EXTRACTED BUS FIELD.** Primary-bus IDSEL bits overlap that field, and > keeping `bus == 1` in the forwarding call **collapses every type-1 destination onto bus 1**. *** PREMISE 4 IS FALSE AS STATED, and the refutation is one function away. *** I wrote that an empty-slot read returns all-ones. `bus_pci_data_access` implements a THREE-WAY contract: read, register 0 -> 0xffffffffffffffff read, any other reg -> ZERO write -> a diagnostic on EVERY access, then returns The measured ID-register instance stands; the GENERAL claim does not. **This matters because it means the candidate dispositions differ TODAY, with no bus-1 device added at all** -- an unconditional all-ones responder differs from the backend at nonzero registers, and announcement policies differ on diagnostic output. (The write diagnostic does not terminate: `fatal()` returns normally.) *** THE DISCRIMINATING ROW I PROPOSED CANNOT DISCRIMINATE, AND IT HAS THREE FALSE-POSITIVE TRAPS. *** At register 0, all-ones is returned by correct forwarding, by the INCORRECT bus-fixed-to-1 forwarding, by explicit all-ones completion, and by announced all-ones completion -- four dispositions, one observable. Worse: * **THE EXISTING ADDRESS DOES NOT ENCODE BUS 1.** `lca_confbus_probe.py`'s setup uses a ZERO window offset, so the recovered tag -- bus field included -- is zero, and the control side reaches the **no-IDSEL fallback to device 0**. *The witness establishes mode-dependent termination, not a correctly addressed secondary-bus transaction.* That is a scope correction to what this row's existing witness is entitled to claim. * **A FAILED LOAD PRESERVES THE CONTROL SIGNATURE.** `memory_rw` pre-zeros, so a handler that returns success without filling data yields zero -- but a literal `return 0` takes the FAILURE path, and `LS_GENERIC_N` then returns *before updating the destination register*, so the witness **reads back the all-ones the register already held.** A vacuity trap of exactly the shape the carrier's witness clauses exist to catch. * **THE PARSER TAKES THE FIRST OBSERVATION** (`printed` uses `re.search`), so adding another print and calling the helper again retrieves the CONTROL's result rather than the new one. **WHAT IT PRESCRIBES INSTEAD:** keep the signature check as an empty-ID COMPLETION check with an independently identified result and a distinct prior destination value, and add a **model-level routing fixture** observing the exact bus/device/function/register passed onward -- distinct synthetic devices on bus 1 and on another bus separate correct decoding from hardcoded bus 1 and from constant-return stubs. Include write dispatch and preservation of primary-bus decoding. *** A SECOND ARCHITECTURAL PREMISE CORRECTED: RAW LCA ABSENCE DOES NOT GUARANTEE ALL-ONES. *** Digital's §6.2.18 says an unanswered transaction is a MASTER ABORT: the read returns *arbitrary data with error status*, raising an instruction exception plus interrupt and IOC error logging. **So the 64-bit all-ones signature is an EMULATOR-COMPATIBILITY oracle, not a hardware contract**, and the round may not claim hardware fidelity for it. The current path delegates to the generic backend and returns success; it implements none of that error sequence. **SCOPE, stated so the round does not overclaim what it closes:** this closes the configuration handler's termination and its missing destination decode ONLY. Still open in the same file -- `lca_ioc`'s unconditional read/write `default` termination and its register-value rejections; `lca_interrupt_assert` / `lca_interrupt_deassert`; and `lca_isa`'s separate guard. Nor does forwarding implement bridge topology or configuration-cycle error reporting: the backend matches a numeric tuple and receives **no cycle-type argument at all**, so type 1 with a zero bus field needs an explicit policy or simple forwarding will alias a root-bus device. **PRIMARY SOURCE, and this project did not have it:** codex cited the *Digital 21066/21066A Hardware Reference Manual* (Table 6-1, §6.4.2, §6.2.18) with page anchors. No 21066/LCA manual was in `_scratchpad/`, and there are several open LCA rows reasoning from source alone. Fetched at the citation, on the `vmesbcp2.pdf` precedent. *** AND THEN VERIFIED LOCALLY RATHER THAN TRUSTED, which is what the carrier's rule demands and which this project has been burned by skipping: `#357`/`#362`/`#365` shipped DDI 0100I page numbers that came from panel output rather than a manual. *** `_scratchpad/21066_66a_hrm.txt`, 713 KB / 13,876 lines: :8840 S6.2.6 "CPU physical address bits <31:7> are used for PCI address bits <26:2>" -> THE SHIFT OF 5 that `relative_addr >> 5` implements. CONFIRMED. :9216 S6.2.9 "PCI address bits ad<1:0> come directly from configuration cycle type register (IOC_CONF, Section 6.4.2) bits <1:0>" -> IOC_CONF selects the CYCLE TYPE and does NOT supply the bus. CONFIRMED. :9486 S6.2.18 "the IOC returns arbitrary data with error status to the CPU, which causes an instruction exception" + internal interrupt + ERR/CODE=1/CMD/ADDR/LOST -> absent-device reads are NOT all-ones on real hardware. CONFIRMED. **One narrowing, stated because a wrong reason gets reused:** codex wrote *"bits 23..2 from CPU address bits 28..7"*. The manual's general sparse rule is the WIDER `<31:7> -> <26:2>` with the same shift; codex's range is the PCI **type-1 config format** (bus 23..16, dev 15..11, fn 10..8, reg 7..2), which S6.2.9 defers to explicitly -- *"restricted by the encoding requirements of PCI configuration cycles as described in the PCI Local Bus [Specification]"*. **Same shift, narrower window, and the narrowing is correct for config cycles** -- so `bus = (tag >> 16) & 0xff` and `dev = (tag >> 11) & 0x1f` rest on the PCI spec's field layout, not on this manual, and the round should say so rather than citing the LCA manual for the field positions. *** A TRAP FOR THE NEXT READER: `file` REPORTS THIS PDF AS "10 page(s)" AND IT IS WRONG. *** The real count lives in a linearized trailer. I nearly discarded the download as truncated because codex had cited `#page=194` and `#page=211`; `pdftotext -layout` settled it in one command. *A size or page check that disagrees with a citation is a reason to extract, not to discard.*open

Post-fix half PENDING (no fix chosen). — note: FILED 2026-09-07. **NOT a new discovery of the SITE** -- [[lcabadval]]'s eleven-kill census already enumerated `:73` and `:85` and called them *"plausibly the most severe of the eleven"*. What was missing is a ROW: the census names them inside a row titled for VALUE GUARDS, which is the census's own closing lesson (*a row named after one class hides the members of the others*), and `OUTSTANDING_BUGS.md` mentioned them **zero** times. **THE SITE, verbatim -- there is no predicate at all:** void lca_interrupt_assert(struct interrupt *interrupt) { fatal("lca_interrupt_assert: TODO\n"); exit(1); } void lca_interrupt_deassert(struct interrupt *interrupt) { fatal("lca_interrupt_deassert: TODO\n"); exit(1); } *** THE WIRING, DERIVED BY READING `DEVINIT(lca)` -- AND IT IS WHAT MAKES THIS SEVERE. *** memset(&interrupt_template, 0, sizeof(interrupt_template)); interrupt_template.line = 0; interrupt_template.name = interrupt_path; /* "<machine>.lca" */ interrupt_template.extra = d; interrupt_template.interrupt_assert = lca_interrupt_assert; interrupt_template.interrupt_deassert = lca_interrupt_deassert; interrupt_handler_register(&interrupt_template); bus_isa_init(devinit->machine, interrupt_path, BUS_ISA_IDE0 | BUS_ISA_IDE1, LCA_ISA_BASE, LCA_ISA_MEMBASE); **The stubs are registered as the handlers for `<machine>.lca`, and `bus_isa_init` is handed THAT SAME PATH together with `BUS_ISA_IDE0 | BUS_ISA_IDE1`.** So the ISA bus -- both IDE controllers included -- routes its interrupts into a function whose entire body is `fatal()` + `exit(1)`. The file's own comment above the stub says *"Line 0 = ISA interrupt."* **WHY IT IS PLAUSIBLY THE WORST KILL IN THE FILE.** Every other terminating call in `dev_lca.c` needs a guest to write a value the model does not expect. **This one needs only that an interrupt is asserted** -- i.e. ordinary disk activity on a machine whose DEVINIT attaches two IDE channels. No unusual value, no undocumented register, no firmware revision. *** WHAT IS ESTABLISHED AND WHAT IS NOT -- read this before quoting the row. *** * **ESTABLISHED, by reading:** the stubs terminate unconditionally; they are registered as the interrupt handlers; `bus_isa_init` receives the same interrupt path with both IDE channels. * **NOT ESTABLISHED:** that any guest actually reaches them. **No measurement has been made.** A device could conceivably never assert on this path, and `interrupt_handler_register` semantics have not been read here. The row does NOT claim "alphabook1 cannot boot"; it claims the wiring is present and the handler is a kill. **NEXT STEP IS A RUNG-3 ATTEMPT, and the apparatus already exists.** `regress/lca_confbus_probe.py` (shipped 2026-09-07 for [[lcaconfbus1kill]]) already boots unmodified `alphabook1` under the debugger with a disk image attached and drives guest `ldq`/`stq` through real decode. The question is whether a guest access can make an IDE channel assert while single-stepping -- **and the carrier's rule cuts against it: a step-based probe sees a SYNCHRONOUS assert (a device handler reached inside the guest's own store) but NOT one that depends on a host-timer callback.** So the honest first question is *what produces the assert*, and if the answer is `timer_add`, this needs a free-running probe rather than a stepped one. **DISPOSITION: option-set MEMBER 7 (IMPLEMENT), and the set's other members do not apply.** There is no value being refused and nothing to decline, accept, mask or fault -- it is an entire path stubbed out. The carrier added member 7 on 2026-09-06 from this very file, using these very functions as its example. A cheaper interim is member 3 (decline + LATCHED announce): return without asserting, announce once, and let the guest see a missing interrupt rather than a dead host -- **but that trades a host kill for a silently lost interrupt**, which is the readback-lie shape [[lcabadval]] is currently held on, so it is a design question and not an obvious win. **TRANSFERABLE PRECEDENT, already closed in this tree:** [[lunaabsentcpu]] -- *"dev_luna88k.c reassert_interrupts() calls the NULL interrupt callback of an UNCONFIGURED cpu slot"* -- same family (a terminating/absent interrupt callback reached by ordinary operation), fixed, and closed with a rung-3 probe witness (`regress/luna_absentcpu_probe.py`). Read that round before designing this one. sev HIGH on the wiring; it would be CRITICAL if a witness lands, and the row says so rather than pre-judging it. *** THE WITNESS-SHAPE QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND FAVOURABLY: THE ASSERT IS GUEST-DRIVEN, NOT HOST-TIMER-DRIVEN, SO A STEPPED PROBE CAN REACH IT. *** The carrier demands one question before designing any probe around a tick: *what produces the thing the tick consumes?* If the answer is `timer_add`, the probe must free-run, because `debugger.c` calls `timer_stop()` while interacting and `step N` returns before `timer_start()`. DEVICE_TICK(wdc) { struct wdc_data *d = (struct wdc_data *) extra; if (d->int_assert) INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq); } **What it consumes is `d->int_assert`, a flag the COMMAND PATH sets from an ordinary guest register write.** No host timer produces it. And tick functions do run while stepping -- `machine.c` decrements `ticks_till_next[te]` by 1 under `single_step` instead of by `N_SAFE_DYNTRANS_LIMIT` -- so the tick fires, one tick at a time. > **PREDICTED ROUTE: a guest write issues a wdc command that sets `int_assert`; the probe steps far > enough for the tick to run; `INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq)` dispatches to the registered handler for > `<machine>.lca`; and that handler is `fatal()` + `exit(1)`.** Synchronous in the carrier's sense > -- what the tick consumes comes from the guest, not from SIGALRM. **STILL A PREDICTION, AND THREE LINKS ARE UNVERIFIED:** (1) that `INTERRUPT_ASSERT` on `d->irq` resolves to the LCA handler rather than to an intermediate ISA controller that swallows it; (2) how many steps the tick needs; (3) whether `alphabook1` reaches a state where a wdc command can be issued from a cold debugger at all. **LINK (1) IS THE ONE TO READ FIRST.** `bus_isa_init` may interpose its own interrupt controller between the IDE channel and the `<machine>.lca` path -- in which case the assert never reaches these stubs, and the row's severity drops sharply. **If it interposes, THAT is the finding, not a failure**, and the row should be re-graded rather than quietly dropped. *Recorded because it converts an open-ended witness question into three named, checkable links.* --- *** A PROCESS NOTE, because it happened while writing THIS paragraph and it is the second instance today. *** The first attempt to record the above went through `python -c '...'` and bash tore the single-quoted string apart on the apostrophes in "guest's" and "carrier's", exactly as it had done hours earlier on a different note. **The rule minted from the first instance -- PROSE DESTINED FOR A RECORD GOES INTO A SCRIPT FILE, NEVER THROUGH `-c` -- was already written down in this same ledger when I broke it again.** That is the carrier's own structure-versus-memory finding landing on me twice in one session: knowing a rule and having it fire on the right object are different problems, and only the second is solved by writing more. This paragraph was written from a file and landed intact on the first attempt. *** LINK (1) IS SETTLED BY READING, AND IT RAISES THE SEVERITY RATHER THAN LOWERING IT. THE INTERPOSED PIC DOES NOT SWALLOW THE ASSERT -- IT FORWARDS IT, AND BOTH STUBS ARE REACHABLE. *** I flagged `bus_isa_init` as possibly interposing a controller that absorbs the interrupt. **It does interpose, and it forwards.** The full chain, every link read: dev_wdc.c DEVICE_TICK(wdc): if (d->int_assert) INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq); -- d->irq is "<machine>.lca.isa.14" (wdc0_irq = 14, wdc1_irq = 15, bus_isa.c:180) bus_isa.c isa_interrupt_assert(): sets the PIC IRR bit for that line, then isa_interrupt_common(d, old_isa_assert) bus_isa.c isa_interrupt_common(): cascades PIC2 -> PIC1 IRQ 2, then new_isa_assert = d->pic1->irr & ~d->pic1->ier; if (old == new) return; if (!new) { INTERRUPT_DEASSERT(d->irq); return; } ... otherwise asserts upward dev_lca.c lca_interrupt_assert() / lca_interrupt_deassert(): fatal("...TODO"); exit(1); **`d->irq` in `bus_isa_data` is the connection made at `bus_isa.c:193`: `INTERRUPT_CONNECT(interrupt_base_path, d->irq)` -- and `DEVINIT(lca)` passes `interrupt_path` = `"<machine>.lca"` as that base path. The 16 ISA lines are registered and the upward connection is made. *** BOTH DIRECTIONS KILL, WHICH I HAD NOT EXPECTED. *** `isa_interrupt_common` calls **`INTERRUPT_DEASSERT(d->irq)`** at the point where the last unmasked IRR bit clears -- and `lca_interrupt_deassert` is the same bare `fatal()` + `exit(1)`. So an ordinary interrupt LIFECYCLE -- assert, then acknowledge -- reaches a terminating stub at BOTH ends. A fix that de-fatalises only the assert leaves the deassert live. **THE ONE REMAINING GATE, and it is NOT a guest-unmask requirement in the direction I first assumed:** the upward assert fires when `pic1->irr & ~pic1->ier` becomes non-zero, i.e. when an IRR bit is set and NOT masked by `ier`. **`ier` is the PIC's interrupt-ENABLE/mask register, and its RESET VALUE has NOT been read here** (`dev_8259.c`). If it starts at 0 -- nothing masked -- then the FIRST IDE assert propagates immediately with no guest setup at all. **That is the next thing to read, and it decides whether this is "reachable after ordinary driver setup" or "reachable immediately".** Recorded as unread rather than guessed. **SEVERITY STAYS HIGH AND IS NOT RAISED TO CRITICAL YET**, because reachability is still established by READING only -- no witness has been run. What has changed is that the plausible-interposition escape hatch is now closed: the PIC forwards, and both stubs are on the path. *** THE LAST GATE IS OPEN AT RESET. THE CHAIN IS NOW COMPLETE WITH EVERY LINK READ, AND IT NEEDS NO GUEST SETUP AT ALL. *** The remaining question was the PIC mask: the upward assert fires when `pic1->irr & ~pic1->ier` goes non-zero, so a non-zero reset `ier` would mask IDE and gate the whole path behind guest driver configuration. Read: dev_8259.c:266 memset(d, 0, sizeof(struct pic8259_data)); dev_8259.c:213 d->ier = idata; <- the ONLY write to ier, from a guest store **`ier` is zeroed at init and is never set anywhere else.** So at reset `ier == 0`, `irr & ~ier` is just `irr`, and **the FIRST set IRR bit propagates upward immediately.** Nothing is masked until a guest deliberately masks it. *** THE COMPLETE CHAIN, EVERY LINK READ IN THE SOURCE: *** 1. dev_wdc.c DEVICE_TICK(wdc): if (d->int_assert) INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq); `int_assert` is set by the guest COMMAND path -- no host timer involved. d->irq is "<machine>.lca.isa.14" (wdc0_irq = 14, wdc1_irq = 15) 2. bus_isa.c isa_interrupt_assert(): sets the PIC IRR bit, calls isa_interrupt_common() 3. bus_isa.c isa_interrupt_common(): new = pic1->irr & ~pic1->ier; ier == 0 AT RESET, so `new` is non-zero on the first assert -> forwards upward on d->irq (and calls INTERRUPT_DEASSERT(d->irq) when the last unmasked bit clears) 4. bus_isa.c:193 d->irq came from INTERRUPT_CONNECT(interrupt_base_path, d->irq), and DEVINIT(lca) passes interrupt_path = "<machine>.lca" as that base path 5. dev_lca.c:70 lca_interrupt_assert(): fatal("...TODO"); exit(1); dev_lca.c:82 lca_interrupt_deassert(): fatal("...TODO"); exit(1); **So on `alphabook1`, an ordinary IDE interrupt ends the host process, and BOTH ends of the interrupt lifecycle -- assert and deassert -- land on a terminating stub.** No unusual register value, no undocumented offset, no firmware revision, and no guest PIC configuration: the mask is open at reset. *** WHAT IS AND IS NOT CLAIMED, because this is the point at which overclaiming would be easy. *** * **ESTABLISHED BY READING, link by link:** the wiring, the forwarding, the open reset mask, and that both stubs terminate unconditionally. * **NOT MEASURED.** No probe has been run. Nothing here shows that a guest on `alphabook1` actually issues a wdc command that sets `int_assert`, nor that the tick runs before the guest does something else. **The row does NOT claim "alphabook1 cannot boot"** -- that is a plausible consequence, not a finding, and it would need a witness. * The severity assessment therefore stays **HIGH on the wiring**. It goes to the top of the critical queue only when a witness lands, and the honest form of that sentence is what this row says rather than what it implies. **A FIX MUST TAKE BOTH STUBS.** De-fatalising only `lca_interrupt_assert` leaves `lca_interrupt_deassert` live on the same path, reached at acknowledge time -- which would convert "dies on the first disk interrupt" into "dies on the first disk interrupt ACK" and read as a fix in every test that only asserts. *Found by following [[lcabadval]]'s own eleven-kill census, which had already named these two as "plausibly the most severe of the eleven" and which nothing had followed up.* *** CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN PRECEDENT CLAIM: [[lunaabsentcpu]] TRANSFERS AS A **WITNESS** TECHNIQUE AND **NOT** AS A DISPOSITION. Checked by reading its diff rather than its title. *** The row above says *"read that round before designing this one"*, which reads as though its FIX transfers. It does not. `79cd12e`'s diff on `dev_luna88k.c` is a **BOUND** repair: - for (cpu = 0; cpu < MAX_CPUS; cpu++) + for (cpu = 0; cpu < d->ncpus; cpu++) /* #503 */ plus a captured `ncpus` snapshot. **luna's defect was walking into UNPOPULATED slots and calling a callback that was the memset's NULL** -- a SIGSEGV from an absent handler. **LCA's defect is a handler that is PRESENT and deliberately terminates.** Bounding a walk cannot help when the walk is correct and the destination is `exit(1)`; there is no unconnected slot here. **WHAT DOES TRANSFER, and it is the more useful half: HOW TO DRIVE AN INTERRUPT FROM GUEST STORES ALONE.** `luna_absentcpu_probe.py`'s witness is *"a guest store of 0xfc000000 to INT_ST_MASK1 followed by a store to SOFT_INT1"* -- **unmask, then trigger, both ordinary guest stores, no host timer and no disk.** That is exactly the shape a witness for this row needs, and it is why the `#503` round is worth reading. **The ISA analogue is not identical**, because there is no soft-interrupt register on this bus: the PIC mask is already open at reset (so the unmask step is free) but the TRIGGER has to come from a device asserting, which is what the reachability census now out to codex is enumerating. *This is the warrant-transfer caution in miniature: a precedent that is genuinely same-family for one purpose (witness construction) can be wrong for another (disposition), and the row title looks identical either way. Read the diff, not the title.* *** MEASURED 2026-09-07. THE MOST SEVERE ITEM IN THIS FILE IS NOW A RUNG-3 WITNESS, AND IT TAKES FOUR GUEST INSTRUCTIONS. *** `regress/lca_irqstub_probe.py`, artifact `regress/artifacts/lcairqstubkill/witness_HEAD_20260907.raw`, sentinel `LCAIRQ_DONE`. lpt ctl yes yes CONTROL: same store, same window, a non-asserting port ok kbc live yes yes DEVICE SIGNATURE: dev_pckbc_access announced the command ok kbc kill dead alive <- THE DEFECT FAIL kbc attrib yes yes ATTRIBUTION ok EVIDENCE: [ pckbc: write to CTL: aa 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 ] EVIDENCE: lca_interrupt_assert: TODO LCAIRQ_RESULT=3/4 **The whole program is four instructions** -- build the scratch pointer, load the port address, load the value, store it -- on unmodified `alphabook1`, and `0xAA` is the STANDARD 8042 SELF-TEST command. No disk image, no OS, no host timer, no driver setup, no unusual value. *** THE MATCHED CONTROL IS WHAT MAKES IT ATTRIBUTABLE, and it is the census that supplied it. *** `lpt ctl` performs the IDENTICAL store -- same value, same width, same K0SEG path, same ISA window -- one port away, at `B+0x378`, where `dev_lpt_tick` is EMPTY and `dev_lpt_access` never asserts. It SURVIVES. So the death is attributable to the DEVICE REACHED, not to storing into ISA space, not to the address width, and not to the debugger path. **TWO PREMISES OF MINE WERE CORRECTED BY THE codex ISA CENSUS BEFORE THIS WAS BUILT**, and the row would have failed without both: the WDC controllers exist ONLY IF an IDE image is attached, so the IDE route this row was written around is unavailable to a probe attaching a memory file; and PIT/RTC asserts are HOST-TIMER driven and therefore invisible to a stepped probe, while PCKBC and the UARTs are synchronous with the guest access. *The census cost one codex invocation and it chose the route.* *** SEVERITY: the wiring claim is now MEASURED, not read. This is a guest-drivable host kill in four instructions through a documented register. *** The row's earlier caution -- "severity stays HIGH on the wiring; it goes to the top of the critical queue only when a witness lands" -- is now discharged on its own terms. **STILL NOT CLAIMED:** that any shipped guest issues an 8042 self-test at that moment. The witness shows the path is open and ordinary, not that a particular OS walks it. **AND THE CONTRACT LIMIT IS THE SAME ONE grok NAMED ON THE SIBLING ROW:** this witnesses THIS `exit(1)`; it is NOT a detector of a repair. "Host survives" would green for a silent return, for a latched announce, and for an actual interrupt implementation alike. **A fix round owes a row that discriminates those** -- and note the deassert stub is on the same path and would need its own. *** TREE-WIDE CENSUS: THIS IS THE ONLY TERMINATING INTERRUPT HANDLER IN THE FORK, 2 OF 70. The sibling grep is discharged with a denominator, and it comes back BOUNDED. *** distinct functions ASSIGNED as an interrupt handler 70 of those, bodies located 70 (no blind spots) whose body calls exit() 2 BOTH in dev_lca.c lca_interrupt_assert dev_lca.c:70 lca_interrupt_deassert dev_lca.c:82 registered handlers that do NOT terminate 68 **So this is NOT a class -- it is the tree's single outlier**, and no sibling hunt is owed. *** AND THE CENSUS WAS RUN TWICE ON PURPOSE, KEYED TWO DIFFERENT WAYS, BECAUSE THE FIRST KEY WAS A CORRELATE. *** Pass 1 matched functions whose NAME ends in `interrupt_assert`/`_deassert` and found **69**. Pass 2 keyed on what actually DEFINES the class -- a function ASSIGNED to `.interrupt_assert` / `.interrupt_deassert` -- and found **70**. **One registered handler does not follow the naming convention and was invisible to the name-keyed pass.** Both agree on the answer (2), but only the second could have been trusted to give it: this project's deriver rule is to key on what makes a member a member, and a name is a correlate whose error is invisible because the output is still a plausible number. *** THE CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX IS THE USEFUL HALF: THERE ARE 68 WORKING PRECEDENTS. *** The codex fix brief asks (Q2) whether an in-tree shape can be copied. The census answers it before the seat does -- 68 registered handlers deliver, latch, forward or ignore an interrupt without ending the process, so the question is not *whether* a non-terminating handler is possible on this architecture but *which* of the 68 shapes suits an Alpha ISA line. **AND IT STRENGTHENS THE CASE THAT THESE TWO ARE UPSTREAM RESIDUE RATHER THAN A DECISION** -- the same reading the option-set rule reached for `sgireunmapped`, where the sibling handlers in the same file already declined and the arm under review was the file's own outlier. Here the outlier is 2-of-70 across the whole fork. *** THE codex FIX DESIGN LANDED AND IT SOLVES THE PROBLEM BOTH WITNESS CONTRACTS DECLARED OPEN. Artifact: `regress/artifacts/lcairqstubkill/codex_fix_20260907.txt`. *** **DENOMINATOR: 36/36 registration call sites in 28 files, 35 assert/deassert pairs = 70 callbacks. That INDEPENDENTLY REPRODUCES this row's own census of 70**, by a different method (registration sites rather than assignment targets). Two derivations, same number. *** 1. MEMBER 7 (IMPLEMENT) IS BLOCKED AT THE DYNTRANS CORE, NOT AT THE DEVICE. *** `alpha_irq_interrupt_assert()` exists and sets `cpu->cd.alpha.irq_asserted = 1`. **But "the only references to Alpha's `irq_asserted` are the two assignments"** -- nothing consumes it -- and `DYNTRANS_RUN_INSTR_DEF`'s interrupt-dispatch block has **ARM, M88K, MIPS, PPC and SH branches and NO ALPHA BRANCH**. So even correct LCA wiring would deliver nothing to guest software. **This independently confirms the filed row [[irqassertedunread]]** -- "alpha, i960 and riscv set cd.<arch>.irq_asserted with no consumer" -- reached from the other direction. A minimal wiring step is still identified and is NOT sufficient on its own: give `lca_data` a connected upstream `struct interrupt`, connect it to `devinit->interrupt_path` (which already defaults to the bootstrap CPU in `device_add()`), and forward both levels. **LCA currently stores no upstream interrupt connection at all**, and passing its own object to the CPU callback would be wrong because `extra` points at `lca_data` rather than the destination CPU. *** 2. MY Q3 FRAMING WAS REFUTED: THERE IS NO HOUSE POLICY FOR THIS CASE. *** I asked which disposition "this tree's own practice favours". The answer is that the precedents CONFLICT: cpu_sh.c sh3_cpu_interrupt_assert/deassert() silent TODO bodies dev_pcc2.c reassert_interrupts() diagnoses, then exit(1) dev_sh4.c sh4_timer_tick() latched announce, then continues *"The SH4 example supports bounded reporting, but it does not establish a universal disposition for an asserted delivery path."* My brief presumed a settled practice; there is none. *** 3. A DISPOSITION I HAD NOT NAMED, WITH AN IN-TREE PRECEDENT: DIAGNOSE AND STOP THE GUEST CPU. *** Not `exit(1)` (host process death) and not a silent or latched return (invisible loss), but an EMULATOR-LIMITATION STOP: `alpha_palcode()` already does exactly this for unsupported PAL calls -- diagnostic plus `cpu->running = 0`. **This is an emulator limitation, not an architectural guest FAULT**, and the distinction is the point. **AND A CAUTION THAT WOULD HAVE MADE A NAIVE FIX SUBTLY WRONG:** *"merely changing `running` inside a device callback does not itself unwind the current batched execution."* `alpha_instr_call_pal()` handles PAL stops by redirecting `next_ic` to `nothing_call`; a device implementation must arrange the same unwind. *That is the same class as the four-readers-proposed-`return` incident -- a plausible edit that skips machinery the enclosing control flow depends on.* *** 4. THE DISCRIMINATING ROW, WHICH IS WHAT BOTH WITNESS CONTRACTS SAID WAS MISSING. *** **"Stopped guest state, plus the reason -- NOT survival."** Proposed acceptance row: starting from a running CPU, an unsupported LCA assertion produces its specific diagnostic and leaves `cpu.running == false`; with debugger-at-end enabled the debugger stays responsive and subsequent steps execute no guest instructions; the matched non-asserting control remains RUNNING. diagnosed guest stop GREEN silent return RED -- CPU remains running latched announce and return RED -- CPU remains running forwarding only, or delivery to a resuming handler RED -- CPU remains running the existing exit(1) RED -- debugger/process is gone **That discriminates all five candidates**, and the state is already observable: `cpu_new()` exposes `running` as a setting, `machine_run()` skips stopped CPUs, and `emul_run()` enters the debugger after all machines stop when debugger-at-end is set. > **SO THE CONTRACT LIMIT ON BOTH LCA WITNESSES IS LIFTED -- for THIS disposition.** Each says > "host survives" cannot tell the fix members apart, and that remains true; the answer is that the > oracle must read the CPU's RUNNING STATE and the diagnostic, not the host's survival. The > existing probes would need that row added; neither has it today. **THE FABLE QUESTION IN §7j-1 IS NARROWED BUT NOT ANSWERED.** I asked whether a latched decline is acceptable for an unimplemented delivery path. codex's answer is that a THIRD option dominates both horns -- but choosing between "stop the guest with a diagnostic" and "lose interrupts quietly and keep running" is still a judgment about what an emulator owes its user, and that is exactly what the flagship seat is held for. **§7j-2 (what observable discriminates) is now ANSWERED and can be struck from the queue when the adjudication runs.** *** THE LOAD-BEARING CLAIM WAS VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY, AND MY FIRST CHECK NEARLY REFUTED IT WRONGLY. *** codex's whole disposition rests on "the Alpha CPU cannot take an asynchronous interrupt". Checked: grep -rn 'alpha.irq_asserted' src/ -> 2 hits, BOTH assignments in cpu_alpha.c the dyntrans interrupt dispatch -> cpu_dyntrans.c tests cd.arm.irq_asserted (:208), cd.m88k.irq_asserted (:212, :382), cd.ppc.irq_asserted (:243) -- and NO cd.alpha. **CONFIRMED.** Nothing consumes the Alpha flag and no dispatch branch exists for it. **MY FIRST CHECK WAS A CORRELATE AND IT FOUND A FALSE POSITIVE.** I grepped `#if defined(DYNTRANS_ALPHA)` in `cpu_dyntrans.c` and got a hit at `:486` -- which is `n_args_to_print` in a DISASSEMBLY function and has nothing to do with interrupts. Read as a refutation, that hit would have produced a confident wrong correction to a seat that was right. **The fix was to search for the THING (an `irq_asserted` test) rather than for a correlate (the architecture ifdef)** -- the deriver rule, on a one-line verification. *** A FACT THIS ROW'S QUESTION DOES NOT CARRY, ESTABLISHED 2026-09-08 FROM THREE INDEPENDENT FILES: OPTION-SET MEMBER 5 (FAULT) IS NOT AVAILABLE ON ALPHA. *** This is an Alpha machine, and the adjudication of this row weighs dispositions from the standing option set. **FAULT looks available and is not**, which is the option-set-completeness problem inverted -- not a missing member, a PHANTOM one. memory_rw.c the device-failure dispatcher has MIPS and M88K exception arms and NO ALPHA ARM (found via dev_lca.c, `lcaisalane`) memory_alpha.c no MM-fault dispatch exists at all (found via `alphapteprot`) cpu_alpha_palcode ALPHA_KENTRY_MM and ALPHA_MMCSR_* are DEFINED and have NO CONSUMERS; kentry[] is written by wrent and initialised to a dummy PAL, never dispatched (found via `alphatbinegsel` Q3) **Three briefs reached this from three directions, none of them asked about it.** And a fourth seat priced it: choosing FAULT obliges building delivery first -- a PAL frame, `kentry[ALPHA_KENTRY_MM]`, MMCSR/VA, and teaching `pc_to_pointers` about a redirected PC. *"That is a new IMPLEMENT round, not a de-fatalisation."* > **SO ANY ANSWER TO THIS ROW THAT REACHES FOR FAULT IS REACHING FOR A ROUND THAT DOES NOT EXIST > YET.** It remains a legitimate ANSWER -- but it is an answer with a prerequisite, and the > prerequisite is large. Recorded here so the adjudication prices it rather than assuming it. *** THE NOTE ABOVE UNDERSTATED THE SCOPE, AND THE CORRECTION IS THE USEFUL PART: FAULT IS NOT "UNAVAILABLE ON ALPHA". IT IS AVAILABLE ON **MIPS AND M88K ONLY**, FOR EVERY ARCHITECTURE IN THIS TREE. Derived 2026-09-08 by opening the dispatcher. *** `src/cpus/memory_rw.c`, the device-failure path -- the whole of it: if (res <= 0 && !no_exceptions) { debug("[ %s device '%s' addr %08lx failed ]"); #ifdef MEM_MIPS mips_cpu_exception(cpu, cache == CACHE_INSTRUCTION? EXCEPTION_IBE : EXCEPTION_DBE, ...); #endif #ifdef MEM_M88K m88k_exception(cpu, cache == CACHE_INSTRUCTION ? M88K_EXCEPTION_INSTRUCTION_ACCESS : M88K_EXCEPTION_DATA_ACCESS, 0); #endif return MEMORY_ACCESS_FAILED; } **TWO `#ifdef` ARMS. There is no ARM arm, no Alpha arm, no PPC arm and no SH arm** -- every other architecture reaches `return MEMORY_ACCESS_FAILED` with no exception delivered at all. > **SO OPTION-SET MEMBER 5 IS A PHANTOM ON EVERY ARCHITECTURE BUT TWO**, and a round on an ARM, SH, > PPC or Alpha device that reaches for FAULT is reaching for a round that does not exist yet. *Found because I wrote the OPPOSITE into a brief. Assessing `fbfiqsilent` -- an ARM footbridge row -- I told the seat that "member 5 FAULT may genuinely be available here, `memory_rw`'s device-failure path has an ARM arm." It replied that the claimed arm **is absent from this tree**, and opening the file confirms it. **I was one brief away from spreading a false availability claim across the ARM queue**, having just corrected three rows for the Alpha version of it.*open

uninorthdevscandev_uninorth.c: `idata & (1 << dev)` at dev==31 is a signed-shift UB, but NOT guest-visible -- the address port is registered with length 4, so idata can never carry bits 32..63 (investigated and DOWNGRADED, not assumed)dev_uninorth.c: `idata & (1 << dev)` at dev==31 is a signed-shift UB, but NOT guest-visible -- the address port is registered with length 4, so idata can never carry bits 32..63 (investigated and DOWNGRADED, not assumed) — witness: none -- READ, not run. The arithmetic and the device registration are established; whether an 8-byte guest access can reach the handler (which is what makes bits 32..63 possible) is NOT established and is the row's open question. — note: FILED 2026-09-07, split out of [[shiftubcensus]] item (A) because it is the only member of that census with a **GUEST-VISIBLE CONSEQUENCE** rather than a language-level one, and it therefore owes a witness the others do not. **THE SITE**, `dev_uninorth.c`, in the PCI address-register write path: :56 uint64_t idata = memory_readmax64(cpu, data, len | MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN); ... :60 d->cur_addr = idata; :70 for (dev=11; dev<32; dev++) :71 if (idata & (1 << dev)) :72 break; **`idata` is `uint64_t` and `1 << dev` is an `int`.** At `dev == 31` that is `0x80000000`, which as a signed `int` is NEGATIVE, so converting it for the `&` against a `uint64_t` **SIGN-EXTENDS it to `0xffffffff80000000`**. > **CONSEQUENCE IF `idata` CARRIES ANY BIT IN 32..63: the loop matches at `dev == 31` when no > device bit is set there, and the scan selects the WRONG DEVICE.** The repair (`1U << dev`) is > therefore NOT behaviour-preserving here -- unlike its sibling in `dev_v3.c`, where the operand's > high bits are provably zero and the same edit changes nothing. **REACHABLE AS A DEVICE:** `machine_macppc.c:68` calls `dev_uninorth_init(machine, machine->memory, 0xe2000000, ...)`, and `dev_uninorth.c:141` registers `"uninorth_pci_addr"` at `addr + 0x800000` = **0xe2800000**. macppc is a supported machine here. *** WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED, AND IT IS THE WHOLE QUESTION: CAN `idata` ACTUALLY CARRY BITS 32..63? *** `memory_readmax64(cpu, data, len | MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN)` returns a value whose width follows the ACCESS WIDTH. On a 4-byte store -- the ordinary way a guest writes a PCI config address -- the result cannot exceed 32 bits, the sign-extended ones meet only zeros, and **nothing observable happens**. The defect needs an **8-byte** access to that register. **So the row is HELD at the reachability question, not at the arithmetic.** A codex analysis is out on exactly this (`regress/artifacts/shiftubcensus/UNINORTH_brief.md`), asking: what does `memory_readmax64` return per width; what widths reach this handler on macppc; and -- the premise I am least sure of -- whether `MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN`, which is OR'd into the `len` PARAMETER, can perturb the length itself rather than only the byte order. **SEVERITY DELIBERATELY LEFT AT `med` PENDING THAT ANSWER.** If an 8-byte access reaches the handler this is a guest-drivable mis-decode on a supported machine and should be HIGH; if it cannot, this collapses into the same language-level hygiene as the other two census members and should be LOW. *Grading it before the answer would be picking the number I prefer.* **THE REPAIR IS ONE TOKEN EITHER WAY** (`1U << dev`), and it is correct under both outcomes -- the question is only what the round may CLAIM, and whether it owes a witness. *** MY SHAKIEST PREMISE IS ANSWERED BY READING, AND IT ANSWERS THE REASSURING WAY -- SO THE ROW NARROWS TO EXACTLY ONE QUESTION. *** I flagged as least certain whether `MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN`, OR'd into the **`len` parameter**, could perturb the LENGTH rather than only the byte order. `src/core/memory.c`: #define MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN 128 (memory.h:98) uint64_t memory_readmax64(struct cpu *cpu, unsigned char *buf, int len) { int i, byte_order = cpu->byte_order; uint64_t x = 0; if (len & MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN) { len &= ~MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN; <- EXPLICITLY STRIPPED byte_order = EMUL_LITTLE_ENDIAN; } ... for (i=0; i<len; i++) { x <<= 8; x |= buf[i]; } **The flag is stripped from `len` before it is used as a count, so it cannot change the length.** And the two cannot collide in practice: the flag is 128 while access widths are 1..8. **WHAT THAT LEAVES, and it is now the WHOLE question:** `x` accumulates exactly `len` bytes, so len == 4 -> x <= 0xffffffff, bits 32..63 are ZERO -> the sign-extended ones meet only zeros and NOTHING OBSERVABLE HAPPENS len == 8 -> x can carry bits 32..63 -> the spurious dev==31 match is REAL > **So the row turns entirely on: can a guest issue an 8-BYTE access to `0xe2800000` on macppc, and > does it reach this handler with `len == 8` intact?** Nothing else matters -- not the endianness > flag, not the arithmetic, both of which are now settled. *Recorded because narrowing a question is worth as much as answering one, and because this half was settled by reading two functions while a seat works the other half. The codex analysis in flight is asked the same thing independently; if it disagrees about the stripping, the disagreement is checkable in four lines.* *** ANSWERED: **NO**. THE ROW IS DOWNGRADED med -> low, AND THE INVESTIGATION IS WHY THE SEVERITY WAS LEFT UNGRADED IN THE FIRST PLACE. *** codex: *"The macppc guest-store paths cannot place bits 32..63 in this register's `idata` or `cur_addr`: the dispatcher clamps the four-byte address window before calling the handler. `MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN` preserves these access widths."* **Both halves verified here rather than accepted:** dev_uninorth.c:141-142 memory_device_register(mem, "uninorth_pci_addr", addr + 0x800000, 4, dev_uninorth_addr_access, d, DM_DEFAULT, NULL); ^-- REGISTERED LENGTH 4 memory_rw.c:495 if (paddr + len > mem->devices[i].length) <- truncates, with the fork's own #91/#93/#94 per-device note above it So an 8-byte guest store to `0xe2800000` is **truncated to 4 bytes before the handler runs**. `memory_readmax64` then accumulates at most 4 bytes, `idata <= 0xffffffff`, bits 32..63 are ZERO, and the sign-extended ones in `0xffffffff80000000` meet only zeros. **Nothing observable happens.** > **SO THIS COLLAPSES INTO THE SAME LANGUAGE-LEVEL HYGIENE AS THE OTHER TWO [[shiftubcensus]] > MEMBERS.** The shift is still UB and still worth the one-token repair; what is retracted is the > claim that it mis-decodes a device. *** THE PROCESS POINT IS THE VALUE HERE. *** The arithmetic was right, the device really is instantiated on a supported machine, and the sign-extension really would select the wrong device -- **every step held except reachability, and reachability is what decided it.** Had the row been graded HIGH on the arithmetic alone it would have carried a guest-visible claim that is false, and a fix round would have been designed around a witness that cannot exist. *Leaving the number blank cost one codex invocation and bought a correct grade.* **A DETAIL WORTH KEEPING:** the sibling `uninorth_pci_data` port at `+0xc00000` IS registered with length **8** (`:143-144`). So the width concern is not absurd in general for this device -- it is simply wrong for the ADDRESS port, which is the one with the shift. A future reader tempted to generalise "uninorth clamps to 4" should not.open

guestsrcunknown_guest-src-openbsd22/ holds 8,138 .c files of contemporary guest OS source covering six of this fork's emulation targets, and NOTHING in the carrier or harness mentions it -- I called a chipset question unanswerable one paragraph before a seat answered it from there_guest-src-openbsd22/ holds 8,138 .c files of contemporary guest OS source covering six of this fork's emulation targets, and NOTHING in the carrier or harness mentions it -- I called a chipset question unanswerable one paragraph before a seat answered it from there — witness: harness: the measured payoff -- lca_pci.c settled lcaconfbus1kill's Q2 and converted its "no shipped guest does this" caution into the opposite finding — note: FILED 2026-09-07. **NOT a defect -- a RESOURCE this project has and does not know it has**, filed because I declared a hardware question unanswerable from this machine one paragraph before a seat answered it from a file on disk. *** `_guest-src-openbsd22/` SITS AT THE PROJECT ROOT AND CONTAINS THE ACTUAL GUEST OS SOURCE. *** Derived rather than transcribed: 8,138 .c files architectures: alpha amiga arc arm32 atari hp300 i386 kbus m68k mac68k mvme68k mvme88k pc532 pmax powerpc sparc sun3 vax wgrisc **Six of those are this fork's own emulation targets** -- `alpha` (alphabook1), `arc`, `arm32`, `mvme88k` (the m88k/luna family), `pmax` (DECstation) and `powerpc` (macppc). It is OpenBSD 2.2, dated 1997, i.e. CONTEMPORARY with the hardware these device models emulate. **IT IS NOT IN THE REPO.** It lives at the project root, outside `GXEMUL-SEC/`, untracked -- which is why nothing in the carrier or the harness mentions it and why a fresh session has no way to learn it exists. *** THE MEASURED PAYOFF, on the day it was noticed. *** Working `lcaconfbus1kill`, I wrote into the ledger that whether `ioc_conf & 1` is a bus selector or a cycle type is *"a statement about the 21066 ... not CHECKED here"*, because `_scratchpad/` holds no LCA datasheet. The codex seat then cited `_guest-src-openbsd22/sys/arch/alpha/pci/lca_pci.c`, and reading it settled the question outright: :103 *bp = (tag >> 16) & 0xff; /* bus */ :106 *dp = (tag >> 11) & 0x1f; /* device */ :127 if (secondary) { ... REGVAL(LCA_IOC_CONF) = 0x01; ... } That is the fix's decode verbatim, plus proof that the register selects the configuration FORMAT. **And it converted the row's own caution -- "NOT CLAIMED: that any shipped guest issues this sequence" -- into the opposite finding: the sequence IS the driver's secondary-bus path.** > **WHY THIS BEATS A DATASHEET FOR THIS PROJECT'S QUESTIONS.** The recurring question here is not > *what does the hardware do* but *what does a guest actually do* -- is a path travelled, is a > register written, does a driver depend on this behaviour. The witness ladder itself ranks a boot > above a probe for exactly that reason ("a probe proves a path CAN be reached; a boot proves it IS > travelled"). **A contemporary driver for the emulated chipset answers that class directly, and it > is greppable in seconds.** **PROPOSED, NOT DONE: a carrier line.** `CLAUDE.md` tells a reader to `ls _scratchpad/*.pdf` before reasoning from first principles about a device, and records that an absent-source note was load-bearing and wrong for twelve days. **This is the same shape one directory over**, and the analogous line would be: *before calling a guest-behaviour or chipset question unanswerable, grep `_guest-src-openbsd22/sys/arch/<arch>/`.* Editing the carrier is an owner-facing act and section J checks its tracked copy, so it is **filed as a candidate for the 2026-09-09 adjudication** rather than done unilaterally. **A CAUTION THAT BELONGS WITH IT:** OpenBSD 2.2 is ONE guest at ONE version. What it does is evidence that a real driver does it; what it does NOT do is not evidence that no guest does. And the fork's models are not obliged to match this driver -- they are obliged to match the HARDWARE, of which this is a well-informed second-hand reading. *Cite it as "the OpenBSD 2.2 driver does X", never as "the hardware does X".*open

armbfiwidthcpu_arm_instr.c X(bfi): `(1 << width) - 1' where width = msb - lsb + 1 ranges [-30,32] -- 468 of 1024 encodable (msb,lsb) pairs reach an undefined shift on a 32-bit-int host, and 465 of those 468 ALSO have architecturally invalid field ordering (msb < lsb); the two sets OVERLAP rather than being disjoint. #510 fixed the SAME expression at UBFX and SBFX and left this third site fifty lines below, and its `== 32' form covers none of the negative widthscpu_arm_instr.c X(bfi): `(1 << width) - 1' where width = msb - lsb + 1 ranges [-30,32] -- 468 of 1024 encodable (msb,lsb) pairs reach an undefined shift on a 32-bit-int host, and 465 of those 468 ALSO have architecturally invalid field ordering (msb < lsb); the two sets OVERLAP rather than being disjoint. #510 fixed the SAME expression at UBFX and SBFX and left this third site fifty lines below, and its `== 32' form covers none of the negative widths — witness: none -- NOT YET ATTEMPTED. The vehicle exists and is cheap: arm_bfx_width_probe.py already plants and executes instruction words on an unmodified machine, so a planted `bfi' with msb < lsb under a UBSAN build is the rung-3 attempt this row owes. This field says `not yet done', never `did not think to ask'. — note: FILED 2026-09-07. **`#510` fixed TWO of THREE sites of one idiom and left the third, whose undefined domain is WIDER than either it repaired.** Found by reading an UNREAD codex answer (`regress/artifacts/queueunrated/codex_bitsbytes_20260907.txt`) that had been sitting on disk, cited nowhere. Every element below was VERIFIED by opening the file, not taken from the seat. *** THE DEFECT. *** `src/cpus/cpu_arm_instr.c`, `X(bfi)` (Bit-Field Insert): int lsb = (uint8_t)ic->arg[2]; int msb = ic->arg[2] >> 16; int width = msb - lsb + 1; x <<= lsb; uint32_t mask = (1 << width) - 1; <-- UNDEFINED over most of its domain **THE DECODE GIVES msb AND lsb INDEPENDENTLY, each 0..31** (verified at the `bfi` arm of the decoder, `(iword & 0x0fe00070) == 0x07c00010`): int lsb = (iword >> 7) & 31; int msb = (iword >> 16) & 31; ic->arg[2] = (msb << 16) + lsb; so **`width` ranges over [-30, 32]** and `1 << width` is undefined three separate ways: width <= 0 negative shift count C99 6.5.7p3 width == 32 count >= width of the promoted type C99 6.5.7p3 width == 31 1 is `int'; 2^31 is not representable C99 6.5.7p4 (signed overflow) *** THE DENOMINATOR, and it is nearly half. *** Of the **1024** encodable (msb, lsb) pairs: 496 nonpositive width (lsb >= msb + 1) -- of which 465 are strictly negative 1 width == 32 (msb=31, lsb=0) 2 width == 31 (msb=lsb+30) --- 499 of 1024 pairs reach an undefined shift **That arithmetic was INDEPENDENTLY DERIVED TWICE and the first attempt was mine and wrong.** A codex answer on a different brief (`codex_shiftub_20260907.txt`) corrected it: *"`msb - lsb + 1 < 0` requires `lsb >= msb + 2`, giving 465 negative widths. Another 31 pairs produce zero; 496 is the number of nonpositive widths."* Recomputed here from the decode: pairs with `lsb >= msb+1` sum to 31+30+...+1 = **496**, and `lsb >= msb+2` sums to 30+29+...+1 = **465**. *The seat was right.* *** WHY THIS IS A SIBLING MISS AND NOT A NEW CLASS. *** `#510` repaired the identical expression at the UBFX and SBFX handlers, which now read: uint32_t mask = (width == 32) ? 0xffffffffU : ((1U << width) - 1); **`X(bfi)` sits about fifty lines below the second of those, in the same file, and was not touched.** The carrier's mechanical rule 2 -- *when correcting a claim, grep for its siblings before calling it fixed* -- is exactly the rule that was missed, and it is recorded there with a prior instance where an "un-fakeable" claim was corrected in one place and survived in three. **The BFX round's own detector cannot see this**: `regress/arm_bfx_width_probe.py` plants UBFX/SBFX words only. **AND THE BFX FIX DOES NOT TRANSFER UNCHANGED.** BFX decodes `width = 1 + ((iword >> 16) & 31)`, so its domain is {1..32} and a `width == 32` special case is sufficient. **BFI's width can be zero or negative, which no `== 32` test catches.** A repair copied from the sibling would close one third of this site's undefined domain and look right. *** WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED, and it is the next step rather than a caveat. *** **No witness has been built and no host misbehaviour has been measured.** UB is not by itself a defect this project ships a fix for without a measurement -- `#510` shipped on a UBSAN differential (1 diagnostic pre-fix, 0 post-fix) plus a source pin, and this row owes the same. The vehicle is cheap and already exists: `arm_bfx_width_probe.py` plants instruction words and executes them on an unmodified machine, so the witness is a planted `bfi` with `msb < lsb` under a UBSAN build. **ARM architecturally leaves `msb < lsb` UNPREDICTABLE for BFI**, so a conforming guest does not emit it. *That is an argument about which guests reach it, not about whether the emulator may invoke host UB when one does* -- which is the same argument `#510` made and shipped on. **PROPOSED FIX (not adjudicated -- no panel has seen this):** uint32_t mask = (width <= 0) ? 0 : (width == 32) ? 0xffffffffU : ((1U << width) - 1); with `mask = 0` for the nonpositive case leaving `rd` unchanged, which is a defensible reading of UNPREDICTABLE and the only one that inserts no bits. **The `x <<= lsb` on the line above is SAFE** (`lsb <= 31` by construction) and must not be "fixed" alongside it. *** CORRECTED 2026-09-08 BY THE codex SEAT, AND THE ERROR WAS MINE. Re-verified by brute force before this edit. *** **499 WAS WRONG. THE TRUE FIGURE IS 468, AND I HAD CONFLATED TWO DIFFERENT QUANTITIES.** width < 0 465 UNDEFINED -- negative shift count width == 0 31 *** DEFINED. `(1 << 0) - 1' is 0. A shift count of ZERO is legal. *** width 1..30 525 defined width == 31 2 UNDEFINED -- signed left-shift result, 6.5.7p4 width == 32 1 UNDEFINED -- count >= width, 6.5.7p3 ---- 468 pairs reaching UNDEFINED BEHAVIOUR 496 pairs with ARCHITECTURALLY INVALID field ordering (msb < lsb) **Those are different sets and I summed the wrong one.** Every nonpositive width is an invalid BFI encoding, but only the strictly NEGATIVE ones are undefined C. *Three derivations agreed on 496 earlier -- and 496 was the right answer to a question I was not asking.* **FOUR MORE CORRECTIONS FROM THE SAME ANSWER:** * **P4 was partly wrong.** `ddi0100i.txt` DOES contain zero `BFI`/`BFC` occurrences, but **its own architecture list includes ARMv6** (verified: *"ARMv4, ARMv4T, ARMv5T, (ARMv5TExP), ARMv5TE, ARMv5TEJ, and ARMv6"*), so calling it "the ARMv5 manual" is inaccurate. BFI/BFC arrive with ARMv6**T2**, which is why they are absent. And *"the broader claim that no other local reference exists remains unestablished."* * **P5 CONFIRMED from the architecture, externally.** ARM's BFI A1 description makes `msbit < lsbit` UNPREDICTABLE, and its constrained behaviour permits **an undefined instruction, a NOP, or an unknown destination value** -- so `mask = 0` is architecturally PERMITTED, not merely defensible. **That settles Q1.** * **P6 needs a host qualification, and it improves the FIX.** `1U` is `unsigned int`, which C99 permits to be 16 bits, so `(1U << width)` is not universally portable either. codex recommends **`1UL` / `0xffffffffUL`**. *** NOTE THIS MAKES `#510`'s SHIPPED REPAIR SUBOPTIMAL TOO -- it uses `1U` -- though harmless on every host this project builds on. *** * **An early `return` IS sound here**, unlike the case the sketch rule was minted from: codex checked the macros -- `X` declares a void function and `Y` generates separate conditional wrappers -- so **there is no handler epilogue for a return to skip.** *The sketch rule says to check the enclosing control flow, not that early returns are always wrong; here the check comes back clean.* *** REACHABILITY IS ESTABLISHED: the BFI decoder branch has NO CPU-model or architecture-version gate ***, and `machine_test.c` registers `testarm` defaulting to SA1110 -- so the site is reachable in the simulator even though that CPU model predates the instruction. **THE WITNESS DESIGN, from Q2, and it kills my one-word plan:** * negative and excessive counts produce **DIFFERENT UBSan messages** (`shift exponent -1 is negative` vs `shift exponent 32 is too large for 32-bit type 'int'`), and width 31 is a *signed result* failure that plain shift-exponent checking MISSES; * **one instruction encoding cannot exercise both count failures** -- the immediate fields fix `width`, and no register contents change it. So the probe needs SEPARATE planted words per class. * **Two apparatus traps, and the first is the error I made twice this session:** *"`session()` consumes child output through its PTY, while callers print parsed results. Grepping the Python process's stderr can miss the sanitizer messages completely."* And: UBSan suppresses repeat reports at an already-reported location, **so diagnostic totals are not execution counts** -- require the intended site and diagnostic CLASS, not a total. *Still outstanding before this can land, in codex's own words: "a fresh BFI sanitizer differential and integration results from binaries tied to this exact tree. I have not measured those or established any host-visible wrong BFI result."* *** THIS ROW CARRIED TWO DIFFERENT DENOMINATORS -- 468 IN ITS TITLE AND 499 IN ITS NOTE -- AND THE NOTE'S WAS THE WRONG ONE. Corrected 2026-09-08, and the correction is the THIRD generation of the same arithmetic. *** The note derived **499 = 496 nonpositive + 2 (width 31) + 1 (width 32)**. **It counted the 31 zero-width pairs as undefined, and they are not**: `width == 0` gives `1 << 0`, which is a perfectly defined shift yielding `mask = 0`. Only *strictly negative* widths are undefined shifts. Re-derived by enumerating all 1024 pairs rather than by arguing: width < 0 465 undefined (negative shift count) width == 0 31 *** DEFINED -- 1 << 0 is 1 *** width 1..30 525 defined width == 31 2 undefined (1 is `int'; 2^31 not representable) width == 32 1 undefined (count >= width of the promoted type) ------------------ UNDEFINED 468 msb < lsb 496 architecturally invalid ordering -- OVERLAPS the undefined set by 465 **So the TITLE's 468 was right all along and the NOTE's 499 was wrong** -- which is the reverse of the usual direction here, where the note corrects the title. **AND THE TITLE'S WORDING WAS ALSO WRONG, in a way the number hid:** it said *"a DIFFERENT 496 have architecturally invalid field ordering"*. **They are not different -- 465 of the 496 ARE among the 468.** The two sets overlap almost entirely; only 31 invalid-ordering pairs (width exactly 0) escape undefined behaviour, and only 3 undefined pairs (widths 31 and 32) have valid ordering. > *** THIS IS THE CARRIER'S OWN "A CORRECTION IS NOT SAFER THAN THE THING IT CORRECTS", THIRD > INSTANCE. *** My first arithmetic was wrong; a codex answer corrected it to 496/465 and I > recomputed and agreed -- **but neither of us asked whether `1 << 0` is undefined**, so the > corrected figure inherited a defect the original question never raised. *A correction carries more > authority than the error, so it earns a second reading, not less of one.* *Found because a DIFFERENT codex brief -- on `armbfcdecode` -- volunteered that "undefined for most encodable widths is incorrect for a 32-bit int: positive widths 1-30 are fine." It was answering question 5 of five, about round scope.* *** FIX DESIGN COMPLETE, codex 2026-09-08 -- AND IT CORRECTED MY ARITHMETIC A SECOND TIME. *** **THE DOMAINS DIFFER, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT.** Derived from each decoder arm rather than assumed: UBFX width = 1 + ((iword >> 16) & 31) domain 1..32 SBFX width = 1 + ((iword >> 16) & 31) domain 1..32 BFI msb, lsb decoded INDEPENDENTLY in 0..31 domain -30..32 So `#510`'s repair is CORRECT at its two sites and INSUFFICIENT here. *** MY "467 OF 468 WOULD REMAIN UNDEFINED" WAS WRONG -- IT IS 465. *** `#510`'s form uses **`1U`**, so `1U << 31` is DEFINED (unsigned, no overflow), and the `width == 32` arm guards the other end. **Verbatim transfer therefore repairs THREE pairs -- two at width 31 and one at width 32 -- leaving the 465 negative-width pairs undefined.** I had assumed the `1U` did not help width 31; it does, and `#510` got that right for handlers that can reach 31. ## THE PATCH /* Emulator choice: msb < lsb leaves the destination unchanged. */ uint32_t mask = (width <= 0) ? 0U : (width == 32) ? 0xffffffffU : ((1U << width) - 1); width pairs current C proposed ----- ----- ---------------- ----------------------------------------- < 0 465 UNDEFINED zero mask; destination unchanged 0 31 defined same zero mask; destination unchanged 1..30 525 defined IDENTICAL mask and insertion 31 2 UNDEFINED mask 0x7fffffffU 32 1 UNDEFINED mask 0xffffffffU (lsb == 0, full-register copy) *** THE Q4 PROPERTY IS ESTABLISHED BY ENUMERATION, NOT ASSERTED -- and it is the part that matters more than the fix. *** *"No currently defined pair changes behavior. For all 556 such pairs the mask is numerically identical ... Enumeration also found zero mismatches against an independently constructed, bit-by-bit field mask across all 1024 pairs."* **So this is a UB repair and not a behavioural change wearing one's clothes** -- which was the risk I flagged. ## THE ORACLE: UBSan, and `build-asan/` ALREADY HAS IT *"The useful runtime observable is a UBSan diagnostic at the offending expression -- not a particular wrong register value."* `build-asan/src/cpus/Makefile` already carries `-fsanitize=address,undefined`, and **ASan alone would NOT detect this arithmetic UB.** *(Confirmed independently: tonight's `build-asan` rebuild log shows `-fsanitize=address,undefined` on the link line, and that tree is currently PART1 CLEAN / PART2_CLEAR.)* **A caution it volunteered and a detector must respect: "468 counts INPUT PAIRS, not expected diagnostic lines."** A row asserting 468 diagnostics would be pinning the wrong quantity. ## SCOPE: still TWO rounds with [[armbfcdecode]] The decoder unconditionally supplies `&cpu->cd.arm.r[rm]` including source field 15; this patch makes no operand-selection change, so it leaves that defect untouched -- *"including at the 525 ordinary, already-defined pairs."* **And it helps the other round: defined mask arithmetic removes a confounder from any subsequent BFC check.** **STATUS: READY TO IMPLEMENT.** Patch supplied, no-behaviour-change property enumerated, oracle named, tree for it already built. **NOT implemented tonight because `#513` is mid-round with an uncommitted working set** -- mixing two rounds in one commit is not a shortcut worth taking. *Unlike [[armbfcdecode]], this round is NOT blocked on a manual: it is a C-semantics repair, and the one architectural question (what `msb < lsb` should do) is answered by an explicit, documented emulator CHOICE rather than by a citation.*open

The row needs a FREE-RUNNING probe, because the ICR INT bit is masked out of every guest-writable arm and its only producer is a host-timer callback that `step' stops#512's detector has a MEASURED clause-(d) escape: a fix that announces correctly and forgets `assert = 0' scores 7/7. The row needs a FREE-RUNNING probe, because the ICR INT bit is masked out of every guest-writable arm and its only producer is a host-timer callback that `step' stops — commits: 9fa07fe — witness: detector:regress/pcc2_c040_probe.py -- the four L2 rows (irq pending, irq live, c040 noassert, c040 noassert2). All THREE clause-(d) mutants that previously swept the instrument are now killed. Artifacts: regress/artifacts/pcc2c040kill/killtable_20260908/ — note: FILED 2026-09-08 as `#512`'s own declared floor breach. **The round graded it a BREACH rather than clause-(e) debt on purpose**: `assert = 0` is the repair's effect, so nulling it is (d)'s canonical form and sits inside the closure. THE SHAPE OF THE REPAIR: breakpoint + `continue` so host-timer callbacks run, T1 enabled with a small compare so a timer interrupt goes pending, MIEN and C040 both set, and the oracle is the `debug("[ pcc2: IPL = %i, MASK = %i => %s ]")` at the foot of reassert_interrupts() reading `no assert`. *That channel IS visible in a stepped capture -- what cannot vary is the STATE, because no guest store can set an ICR INT bit.* *** THE ORACLE THIS ROW WAS FILED WITH IS WRONG, AND THE codex SEAT HAD ALREADY SAID SO IN AN ANSWER I HAD RECORDED AS "not yet fully mined". Corrected 2026-09-08, VERIFIED BY LINE ORDER. *** The row proposed reading `debug("[ pcc2: IPL = %i, MASK = %i => %s ]")` for `no assert`. **That message EXECUTES BEFORE BOTH SUPPRESSIONS:** :334 debug("[ pcc2: IPL = %i, MASK = %i => %s ]" ...) <-- prints `assert' HERE :339 if (!(GENCTL & PCC2_MIEN)) assert = 0; :364 if (GENCTL & PCC2_C040) { ... assert = 0; } :374 if (assert) INTERRUPT_ASSERT ... else INTERRUPT_DEASSERT So it reports the PRE-suppression value and is **green under exactly the mutant it would be chosen to catch**. codex: *"do not use the existing `IPL ... => ASSERT' debug message as the line-state oracle: it executes before MIEN suppression and before the proposed C040 suppression. Observe the interrupt callback/state."* > **THE CORRECT ORACLE IS THE INTERRUPT CALLBACK/STATE, not the diagnostic.** A free-running probe > is still required for the STATE (an ICR INT bit cannot be set by a guest store), but the CHANNEL > changes: observe delivery, or instrument the callback -- never the pre-suppression debug line. *This is the channel-line check failing on a row I wrote while quoting the channel-line check. A row whose named channel cannot vary under its named mutant is vacuous by construction -- and here the channel was not merely invariant, it was measured at the wrong POINT IN THE FUNCTION.* *** THE "NEEDS A FREE-RUNNING PROBE" WARRANT IS WRONG. Refuted at pass 2 by grok and VERIFIED here 2026-09-08. *** `pcctwo_interrupt_common()` ORs `PCC2_IRQ_INT` onto SCSIICR/SCCTX/SCCRX when those lines assert, and `dev_clmpcc.c:88-89` calls `INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq_scc_tx)` **synchronously inside a guest store to CLMPCC_REG_IER**; `machine_mvme88k.c` constructs clmpcc with its irq wired to pcc2. **So the state is reachable while single-stepping** -- `st.b` IEN|IL to SCCTX, `st.b` to the clmpcc IER, `st.b` `C040|MIEN` (0x06) to GENCTL. **THIS ROW IS THEREFORE AN IN-ROUND L2 OBLIGATION, NOT A FILED ONE**, and `pcc2c040kill` has been reopened accordingly. The remaining difficulty is the ORACLE, not the state: the `debug()` line is before both suppressions, so the observable must be the interrupt line itself -- `INTERRUPT_ASSERT` / `cpu->cd.m88k.irq_asserted` / guest delivery. *Two wrong reasons in a row on this same question -- first "the channel is invisible" (false: it prints while stepping), then "the state is unreachable" (false: another device's store sets it). The conclusion "no row today" was right both times and neither reason was.* *** THE VEHICLE EXISTS AND IS SHIPPED. `regress/m88k_exc_probe.py` IS ALREADY AN m88k FREE-RUNNING EXCEPTION-DELIVERY PROBE. Found 2026-09-08 by looking instead of reasoning. *** Its own header describes the shape this row needs, verbatim: > *"seeded with `rN=`, a `br .` (c0000000) planted at every vector entry so a delivered exception > spins rather than executing zeros, `breakpoint add <8*vector>`, `continue`, then `reg` and > `reg 0,0`."* **So the repair is a COPY of a proven in-tree shape, not a new capability.** That matters for the disposition: "needs a different probe shape" sounded like a capability gap and is really a half-day's careful work against an existing template. **THE ORACLE, now that both halves are settled:** STATE (stepped-reachable, per grok/pass 2) st.b IEN|IL -> SCCTX; st.b -> CLMPCC_REG_IER, whose handler calls INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq_scc_tx) synchronously inside the store; pcctwo_interrupt_common() then ORs PCC2_IRQ_INT into SCCTX. ORACLE (needs FREE-RUNNING) the m88k INTERRUPT vector entry. Plant `br .' there, `breakpoint add', `continue'. Breakpoint FIRES = the line asserted = the mutant. Loop survives to timeout = suppressed = the fix. > **WHY THE ORACLE STILL NEEDS FREE-RUNNING EVEN THOUGH THE STATE DOES NOT** -- and this refines > grok's *"the obstacle is the oracle, not the state"* rather than contradicting it. The only > difference between the fix and the mutant is `INTERRUPT_ASSERT` versus `INTERRUPT_DEASSERT` on > `d->cpu_irq`; `cpu->cd.m88k.irq_asserted` is a HOST-side field with no guest-readable reflection, > so the sole guest-visible consequence is DELIVERY -- and `cpu_dyntrans.c` suppresses interrupt > dispatch while single-stepping by design (*"Do not cause interrupts while single-stepping"*). > **State: stepped. Delivery: free-running. Both facts are needed and neither alone settles it.** *Note the adjacency to `m88kexcdetectorl2`, which is a HIGH row about that same probe. These are separate rows and must not be merged -- same vehicle, different defect, different oracle.* *** THE DESIGN REVIEW CAUGHT TWO DEFECTS BEFORE A LINE WAS WRITTEN, AND THE FIRST IS THAT THE ROW WOULD HAVE PASSED ITS OWN MUTANT. codex, 2026-09-08, VERDICT: BUILD-WITH-REVISIONS. *** ### 1. *** THE PROPOSED DEFECT ROW STILL PASSES THE `return` MUTANT. *** **GENCTL resets to ZERO**, so MIEN is clear throughout the setup and every completed recalculation DEASSERTS the CPU line. At the final GENCTL write: shipped repair deasserts the line -> no interrupt PASS `assert = 0' DELETED asserts the line -> interrupt caught `assert = 0' -> `return' leaves the line UNCHANGED -> no interrupt *** PASSES *** > *"Deleting the assignment PERMITS ASSERTION; returning PRESERVES THE INCOMING LINE STATE. The > callbacks simply assign `irq_asserted = 1` or `0`; returning invokes neither."* **My §3 treated the two mutants as interchangeable. They are not**, and the row was built around the one that happens to be easier to catch. **THE FIX IS A PRECONDITION, not a new oracle: write MIEN-ONLY GENCTL IN BOTH ROWS FIRST**, so the CPU line is already ASSERTED before the operation under test. Then `return` leaves it asserted, the interrupt is delivered, and the row reddens. ### 2. *** THE ORACLE WAS A CHECK THAT CANNOT FAIL. VERIFIED IN THE CODE. *** `session()`'s `rd()` tests `until in buf` **against the ENTIRE ACCUMULATED TRANSCRIPT**, at the top of its loop -- and `alive = rd(settle)` has already drained the boot banner, which ends at a `GXemul>` prompt. So `("continue", grace, "GXemul>")` returns **True with ZERO READS**. codex exercised the extracted reader in memory and got exactly that. **And `how == "no-breakpoint"` is not the negative oracle I took it for**: it establishes a MISSING TOKEN, not successful execution without delivery. The runner deliberately preserves that status through forced termination and unreaped outcomes, *"so a C040-specific hang or unexpected guest halt can satisfy a timeout-only negative oracle."* ### 3. THE REVISED DESIGN (to build) 1. Fresh machine per row; perform setup while STEPPING. 2. Establish the pending SCC TX request, then write **MIEN-only GENCTL in BOTH rows** -- this is the precondition from §1. *Do not rewrite SCCTX afterwards: its write arm CLEARS INT.* 3. Final GENCTL write: MIEN-only for the control, MIEN|C040 for the defect row. 4. `continue` into a FINITE guest path with a **separate normal-completion breakpoint**. The control must stop at the interrupt entry; the defect row must reach NORMAL COMPLETION without hitting it. **That gives the negative case affirmative evidence instead of a timeout.** 5. Attribute stops by FRESH breakpoint evidence and PC. **Treat timeout, unexpected stop or death as FAILURE**, never as the negative result. ### 4. EVERY HARDWARE PREMISE CONFIRMED, one with a better warrant than I had * **PSR `0x80000000`** keeps supervisor mode, clears IND and SFRZ, preserves endianness; the dispatch condition is `irq_asserted && !(PSR & IND)` outside single-stepping. **It also checked my `stcr` word against the decoder** -- it does select `stcr r5,cr1`. *That is the hand-assembled-encoding trap closed by someone other than its author.* * **VBR = 0 is right, and for a better reason than mine:** `mvmeprom.c:59` EXPLICITLY sets it to zero, rather than it being an assumed reset value. * **Entry `0x8`**: interrupt is vector 1 and entry sets PC to `VBR + 8 * vector`. * **Source and priority:** SCCTX takes `0x13`; a qualifying IER write asserts SCC TX synchronously, making it `0x33`; recalculation selects IPL 3; MASK starts at 0, so the comparison succeeds. ### 5. TWO CORRECTIONS TO MY OWN Q2 EXPECTATIONS * **"Suppression by another route" is NOT inherently a defect.** *"A behaviorally equivalent implementation should pass. The defect is violated behavior or collateral state changes, not failure to use the local variable named `assert`."* * **My "both rows fail to deliver" escape is not a green pair** -- `(no interrupt, no interrupt)` FAILS the positive control. It becomes an escape only if the grader omits or neutralises that control failure, which is an argument for asserting the control's outcome explicitly rather than treating it as informational. **Residual classes it names as still uncovered by a delivery-only pair:** C040 suppression that corrupts MASK/MIEN/pending state or IPL bookkeeping; suppression that stays stuck after C040 clears (needs a RECOVERY observation); and suppression that works only for the tested source, priority or first invocation. *** CLOSED 2026-09-08. ALL THREE ESCAPING MUTANTS ARE KILLED. *** BASE 11/11 M_d1_noassert 9/10 `assert = 0' DELETED -- was 7/7 (a CLEAN SWEEP) KILLED M_return 9/10 `assert = 0' -> `return;' -- the one-token pass-2 mutant KILLED M_latchinside 10/11 `assert = 0' INSIDE the latch -- was 10/10 KILLED **The rows, and what each buys:** irq pending SCCTX reads 0x33 after the clmpcc IER store -- LIVENESS. Without it, "no interrupt" is indistinguishable from "no pending request was ever created". irq live C040 CLEAR: the guest REACHES the interrupt vector (pc = 0x8). POSITIVE CONTROL, and it is what makes the negative case meaningful. c040 noassert C040 SET on an ALREADY-ASSERTED line: reaches COMPLETION (pc = 0x1001c). c040 noassert2 the SECOND C040 encounter, latch already set: also reaches completion. *** TWO DESIGN CORRECTIONS MADE THIS WORK, AND NEITHER WAS MINE. *** 1. **The precondition.** My first design wrote C040 into a RESET GENCTL, so MIEN was clear, the line was already deasserted, and `return` -- which merely preserves the incoming line state -- would have PASSED. Writing MIEN-only GENCTL FIRST, in BOTH rows, is what makes it catchable. *codex, design review, before a line was written.* 2. **The encounter axis.** `assert = 0` moved inside the latch suppresses correctly on the FIRST encounter and skips it on every later one, so a single-encounter row scores 10/10 against it. **Closing the axis with one repeated write beats adding a row per mutant** -- the class-closure rule rather than pass-per-instance. *Predicted by codex on pass 1, measured here.* **AND THE NEGATIVE CASE IS AFFIRMATIVE, NOT A TIMEOUT.** Both outcomes stop at a breakpoint and the discriminator is WHICH PC. The obvious oracles were both unusable: the `debug()` line executes BEFORE the suppressions, and `("continue", grace, "GXemul>")` returns True with ZERO READS because `rd()` matches against the whole accumulated buffer, which already holds a prompt. **RESIDUAL, disclosed rather than implied:** these four rows establish DELIVERY under one source, one priority and two encounters. They do not cover C040 suppression that corrupts MASK/MIEN/pending state, suppression that stays stuck after C040 CLEARS (a recovery observation), or other sources and priorities. *And per codex: suppression by a different implementation route is NOT a defect -- "the defect is violated behavior or collateral state changes, not failure to use the local variable named `assert`."* *** COMMITTED AS `9fa07fe`, inside `#512`. This row was FILED as coverage debt and CLOSED IN-ROUND instead, which is what pass 2 required. *** It never became a separate round: the four rows it specified ship as part of the detector they were owed to.fixed
